title: Load Balancers Terminate Connections: What That Does to Source IPs, Health Checks, and Draining
metaDescription: A complete technical breakdown of what a load balancer actually does to a TCP connection: connection termination versus passthrough, why source IP preservation is a configuration decision and not a default, how health check traffic differs from real traffic, connection draining and deregistration delay, and a real case study of a team debugging the wrong layer for intermittent drops.
excerpt: Every layer in this series so far assumed the connection hitting your security group belongs to the client. It doesn't, not once a load balancer sits in front of the instance. The load balancer ends the client's connection and opens a new one of its own. This is what that actually changes, at the packet level, and why teams debugging intermittent drops keep looking at the wrong layer.

faqs.q: Does an NLB always preserve the client's source IP?
faqs.a: By default, yes, for instance targets and IP targets in the same VPC, because NLB operates at layer 4 and typically forwards the original packet rather than terminating the TCP connection. Cross-zone routing to IP targets in a different VPC, or client IP preservation being explicitly disabled on the target group, breaks this. Always check the target group's client IP preservation attribute directly rather than assuming it based on NLB versus ALB.

faqs.q: Why does my security group rule allowing traffic from a specific client IP stop working after adding a load balancer?
faqs.a: Because the connection your instance now receives originates from the load balancer's own network interface, not the client. Any security group rule written against a client CIDR needs to move to the load balancer's security group instead, and the backend's security group should allow traffic from the load balancer's security group by reference.

faqs.q: Should I set the deregistration delay to zero for faster deployments?
faqs.a: No. A zero deregistration delay stops routing new connections to the instance immediately but does not guarantee in-flight requests finish, and some load balancer implementations will forcibly close connections still in progress. A short delay, long enough to cover your slowest realistic request plus a margin, is the safer default. Tune it against your actual p99 request duration, not a guess.

faqs.q: Why do health checks show the instance as healthy while real users report errors?
faqs.a: Health checks hit a specific, usually lightweight path with no cookies, no keep-alive reuse, and no payload, so they can pass while a real request path involving a database call, a session lookup, or a larger payload times out or fails. A health check only proves the checked path works, not that the service works.

title: Iptables, Nftables, and Conntrack: What's Actually Enforcing Your Security Group
metaDescription: A complete technical breakdown of Linux packet filtering: netfilter hooks, iptables tables and chains, the iptables to nftables migration, how conntrack actually tracks connection state, stateless vs stateful filtering, and a real case study of a local firewall rule silently undoing a correctly configured AWS security group.
excerpt: A security group is a suggestion the moment traffic crosses the network interface. The kernel makes the real decision, packet by packet, through netfilter, iptables or nftables, and a connection tracking table that remembers every flow your server has ever touched. This is that layer, in full.

title: The Most Expensive Part of Your Agent Stack Is Also the Least Predictable
metaDescription: A technical breakdown of why frontier LLMs shouldn't sit at every layer of your agent stack, with architecture diagrams, cost tables, a security layer, a migration case study, and a model selection guide.
excerpt: Routing, model selection, and task assignment are bounded decisions. They don't need a frontier model, they need a policy. Architecture, cost tables, a security layer, a real migration case study, and a model shopping list.
tldr: Most agent platforms route every decision through a frontier LLM, including ones that are just bounded classification problems. Production systems use a tiered architecture instead - deterministic code for anything rule-based, fine-tuned small models for narrow repetitive tasks, custom models trained on curated traffic, and frontier models reserved for genuine open-ended reasoning. This post covers the architecture, cost math, security guardrails placement, a migration case study with before/after numbers, and a concrete model selection table by tier.

title: Security Groups Explained: The Firewall Rule That Outlives Every Project
metaDescription: A complete technical deep dive into AWS security groups: stateful vs stateless filtering, connection tracking, rule anatomy, security groups vs NACLs, real production configurations, audit commands, and why misconfigured rules survive project handoffs.
excerpt: A security group is a stateful firewall attached to your instance's network interface. This is a complete breakdown: what it is, why it works the way it does, how packet evaluation actually happens, real production examples, and the delivery handoff pattern that turns a temporary rule into a breach.

faqs.q: If a security group has no deny rules, how do I block a specific malicious IP?
faqs.a: You can't, with a security group alone. Security groups are allow-only. To block a specific CIDR range you need a NACL deny rule at the subnet boundary, which is stateless and evaluated by rule number.

faqs.q: Does deleting a security group rule immediately close an active connection?
faqs.a: No. Connection tracking means an already-established connection keeps flowing until it closes naturally or the conntrack entry expires. Removing the rule only blocks new connections. To kill a live session you need to terminate the connection itself or use a stateless NACL deny, which applies immediately.

faqs.q: Why does the outbound rule matter if security groups are stateful?
faqs.a: Return traffic bypasses outbound rules automatically, but traffic your instance initiates does not. Tightening outbound rules limits what a compromised instance can reach or exfiltrate to, which is exactly the traffic that matters during an incident.

faqs.q: We're a freelance/agency team shipping infra for clients. What's the actual fix for the handoff problem?
faqs.a: Either leave a handoff document listing every open rule, its reason, and who to contact, or keep a retainer where someone is still watching the account. The twenty-minute audit in this post is the minimum bar before any handoff.

title: I Gave an AI Direct Write Access to My Codebase. Here's the Architecture.
metaDescription: How I built a self-hosted MCP server inside a Next.js portfolio app that gives Claude direct read/write access to the GitHub repo: architecture, debugging, and the stateless transport bug that took an hour to find.
excerpt: Most developers use AI as a text generator. I wired Claude directly into my portfolio repo, and it can now read, write, and commit any file without me touching a keyboard. This is how the MCP server works, what broke during the build, and why server.close() was the culprit.
tldr: Built a stateless MCP server as a Next.js API route. It proxies Claude tool calls to the GitHub Contents API, giving an AI agent direct commit access to the repo. The bug that broke it: calling server.close() before the async transport Promise resolved.

faqs.q: Is this safe? Claude has write access to your entire repo?
faqs.a: The GITHUB_TOKEN lives in Vercel's environment variables, never in the codebase or chat. The MCP endpoint has no auth of its own: the security model is that only Claude.ai (with the connector configured) can reach it, and Claude operates under its own safety constraints. For a personal portfolio this is an acceptable risk. For a production app with customer data you'd add an API key or OAuth layer on the MCP endpoint itself.

faqs.q: Why not just use the official GitHub MCP?
faqs.a: The official GitHub MCP exists but isn't in Claude's integration marketplace yet. Self-hosting inside the existing Next.js app meant zero additional infrastructure: the MCP server deploys with the portfolio on every git push to main.

faqs.q: Why is the transport stateless? Doesn't that lose context between tool calls?
faqs.a: MCP context lives in the Claude conversation, not in the server. Each tool call is a fresh HTTP request with all the information it needs in the request body. Stateless is correct here, since it's the serverless-friendly design and it's what lets Vercel handle it without sticky sessions.

faqs.q: Can I use this pattern for my own portfolio or project?
faqs.a: Yes. The full pattern is: Next.js API route + WebStandardStreamableHTTPServerTransport + GitHub Contents API + GITHUB_TOKEN in env vars. The key constraint is don't call server.close() before transport.handleRequest() resolves: that's the bug that killed the tool list.

title: Scripts Are Not Shortcuts. They Are Architecture.
metaDescription: Why npm scripts are a form of architecture, not just aliases: a deep dive into how a real monorepo uses scripts to encode decisions about how a project is run, validated, and shipped, plus the Bash and Linux process mechanics underneath, including how to safely stop a script you didn't mean to run.
excerpt: npm scripts are not aliases. They are the interface between a developer's intent and a system's behaviour. Here's how a real production monorepo uses over fifty scripts to encode decisions about how it runs, validates itself, and ships, plus what actually happens on the machine when a script runs and how to stop one cleanly.
tldr: npm/pnpm scripts are architecture, not shortcuts: they encode how a project runs, builds, tests, and ships behind a stable name. Running one spawns a real subshell with node_modules/.bin on PATH, so exit codes, shebangs, and signals all behave like any other Linux process. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the foreground job; for backgrounded or orphaned processes (like a stuck dev server on a port), use jobs/fg/kill or lsof + kill, trying SIGTERM before SIGKILL. A minimum viable script set is three: dev, lint (auto-fix), build (single source of truth for compilation).

title: How I Built an Offline-First Event Platform Using BLE Mesh Networking
metaDescription: How I designed a production-grade offline-first event management app using BLE mesh networking, Kalman filtering, and hybrid transport layers, without any internet dependency.
excerpt: Most apps assume the internet exists. I built one that doesn't. This is how I architected OurStoryz, a production event platform that works fully offline using BLE mesh networking, Kalman filtering for RSSI-based positioning, and hybrid transport layers.

faqs.q: Does this work on both iOS and Android?
faqs.a: Yes. Both platforms support concurrent BLE advertising and scanning (dual Central/Peripheral role), but the API surface is different enough to require an abstraction layer. The hybrid transport logic handles iOS-specific Multipeer Connectivity alongside the cross-platform BLE and Wi-Fi Direct layers.

faqs.q: What's the practical range of the mesh?
faqs.a: BLE range is roughly 10-30m per hop depending on environment. Wi-Fi Direct extends this to ~200m for paired devices. Because messages can hop peer-to-peer across the mesh, a 300-person venue is fully covered even if no two devices are directly in range: the network finds a route.

faqs.q: How do you handle messages sent while a device is outside the mesh?
faqs.a: Every outgoing message is persisted in a local Realm DB queue before transmission. If the device is out of range or the transport fails, the retry worker picks up pending messages every 5 seconds when the app is foregrounded. Messages with 5 failed attempts are marked failed and surfaced to the user.

faqs.q: Can you build something like this for my project?
faqs.a: Yes. BLE mesh, offline-first architecture, and hybrid transport systems are core work I've shipped in production. If your product needs to operate in RF-hostile or connectivity-uncertain environments, reach out and we can scope what the architecture looks like for your use case.

title: Junior Devs Are Not Losing Jobs to AI. Mid-Level Devs Are.
metaDescription: Everyone says AI will replace junior developers first. They're wrong. The developers actually at risk are mid-level engineers, here's why.
excerpt: The conventional wisdom is wrong. AI is not eating junior developer roles first, it's compressing the mid-level skill premium out of existence. Here's what's actually happening on engineering teams right now.

faqs.q: Are juniors actually safe? Or is this more nuanced?
faqs.a: Not entirely. Juniors at risk are the ones who treat AI as a search engine rather than a tool they critically evaluate. A junior who understands why generated code works, catches the subtle type errors, and pushes back on bad output is more valuable than a mid-level coasting on pattern recognition.

faqs.q: How do you define 'going senior' beyond just job title?
faqs.a: Senior is not a title, it's an architectural scope. The clearest signal: are you the person who implements what others spec, or the person who determines what gets built and why? If it's the former, you're still in mid-level territory regardless of your years or pay grade.

faqs.q: What are the safest niches to specialise in right now?
faqs.a: Legacy systems with no AI training data, hardware-adjacent work where latency and device APIs matter, high-accountability systems where a human has to own the decision, and domain-specific architecture that requires organisational context. These are the niches AI is structurally bad at.

title: You Don't Have a Skill Problem. You Have a Visibility Problem.
metaDescription: Most skilled developers are invisible to the clients and companies they want to work with. The problem isn't skill, it's that nobody knows you exist.
excerpt: I've talked to developers with five years of production experience who can't land a remote contract. And I've seen two-year developers charging $150/hour. The difference is not skill. It's visibility.

faqs.q: What's the minimum viable visibility stack for a developer who's starting from zero?
faqs.a: A GitHub profile with documented real projects, one deep public case study with real numbers, and a LinkedIn headline that names a specific outcome rather than a role title. In that order. The case study does the most work: it's searchable, shareable, and self-validating in a way a resume never is.

faqs.q: How do you write a case study that actually converts, not just impresses other developers?
faqs.a: Start with the problem, not the tech. "I built a BLE mesh event platform" is a topic. "I built an event platform that works with no internet for 300 people in a signal-hostile venue" is a story with a client on the other end of it. Every case study should have: the problem, the constraint, your approach, the measurable outcome.

faqs.q: Is content marketing or a case study more important for inbound?
faqs.a: Both, but in the right order. A case study gets you found by people who already have the problem. LinkedIn content builds recall and trust with people who don't have the problem yet but will. The case study is the floor: it has to exist before the content amplification is worth doing.

title: Offline-First Is Not a Feature. It's an Architecture Decision You Can't Bolt On Later.
metaDescription: Developers treat offline support as a feature to add before launch. It's not, offline-first is a foundational architectural decision that shapes every layer of your app.
excerpt: We'll add offline support before launch" is the engineering equivalent of "we'll add tests after it's working." It reveals a misunderstanding of what offline-first actually is. Here's what it costs to get this wrong.

faqs.q: Which conflict resolution strategy is right for my app?
faqs.a: Last-write-wins is simplest and works when concurrent offline edits to the same record are rare and recoverable. Server-authoritative is safer for high-stakes state (check-ins, payments). CRDTs are the right answer when you need true concurrent merges but they add significant implementation complexity. Pick based on what a conflict actually costs.

faqs.q: What's the best local database for offline-first React Native?
faqs.a: Realm and WatermelonDB are the two serious options for React Native. Realm has better out-of-the-box sync if you're using Atlas Device Sync. WatermelonDB is lighter and more flexible for custom sync layers. For pure SQLite control, op-sqlite is worth evaluating. The choice matters less than committing to it early.

faqs.q: Does offline-first apply to web apps too, or just mobile?
faqs.a: The architecture is the same. Local DB as source of truth, background sync, queued mutations, conflict resolution policy. The implementation layers differ (IndexedDB instead of Realm, Service Workers for background sync), but the data flow inversion is identical. Progressive Web Apps with offline-first architecture follow the same principles.

title: Stop Using TypeScript Like It's JavaScript With Spellcheck
metaDescription: Most developers are using TypeScript wrong, treating it as optional documentation rather than a structural tool. Here's what real TypeScript usage looks like and why it matters.
excerpt: The 'any' type is a lie you tell TypeScript so it stops asking questions. Every codebase I've walked into that claimed to be "written in TypeScript" has had the same anti-patterns. Here's what TypeScript looks like when used as an architecture tool.

faqs.q: What are the most common TypeScript anti-patterns you see in real codebases?
faqs.a: The most common ones: using `any` at API boundaries, not enabling `strict` mode in tsconfig, defining types as interfaces with all optional fields, and typing function return values as `object` or `unknown` without narrowing. All of these give TypeScript the shape of safety without the substance.

faqs.q: How do you tighten TypeScript in a legacy codebase without a full rewrite?
faqs.a: Enable `strict: true` in tsconfig. Run `tsc --noEmit` in CI. Set a policy that `@ts-ignore` requires a written justification comment. Start tracking the count of `any` in the codebase as a metric. None of these require a rewrite: they surface where the type system is being bypassed.

faqs.q: Which of these patterns is most worth adopting first?
faqs.a: Discriminated unions and the exhaustive `never` check are the two that pay back most consistently. Branded types are invaluable on any codebase handling multiple kinds of IDs or domain primitives. State machine types eliminate an entire class of UI bugs around loading/error/success state.
